By: Dhanak and Associates

Being served with a legal notice or summoned to court for a case you know is completely fabricated is an overwhelming and distressing experience. At Dhanak and Associates, we frequently encounter clients who are targeted by malicious litigation—whether it is a false FIR, a fabricated civil suit, or a trumped-up matrimonial dispute.

 Remedies Against False Cases

1.  Quashing of FIR (Section 482 of the CrPC/Section 528 of the BNSS):
    If a false FIR has been registered against you, you can approach the High Court under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure

2.  Anticipatory Bail (Section 438 of the CrPC/Section 482 of the BNSS):
    If you fear arrest due to a false criminal complaint, you can apply for anticipatory bail.

3. Defamation Suit:
    If the false case has tarnished your reputation, you have the right to file a civil suit for damages for defamation. You can claim compensation for the mental agony, loss of reputation.

Section 211 of the IPC (False charge of offence made with intent to injure):
    This is the primary section used to penalize individuals who institute criminal proceedings knowing there is no just or lawful ground. If the false charge carries a punishment of death or life imprisonment the accuser can be punished imprisonment of up to 7 years.

Mutual Divorce in India: A Complete Guide
 
Before filing for mutual divorce, couples must satisfy certain conditions. There should be no coercion, fraud, or undue influence compelling either spouse to agree.

Under the Hindu Marriage Act, the couple must have been living separately for at least one year before filing the petition. "Living separately" does not necessarily mean living in different cities or houses — it means they have not been living as husband and wife. The separation can be under the same roof, provided they have ceased to cohabit as a married couple.

Additionally, they should have settled all ancillary matters, including alimony, maintenance, child custody, and division of property, before or during the proceedings

Filing the Joint Petition (First Motion):Both spouses jointly file a divorce petition before the Family Court having jurisdiction — typically the court in whose jurisdiction they last resided together, where the marriage was solemnized.

The Cooling-Off Period: After the first motion is recorded, the court traditionally imposes a cooling-off period of six months.

Second Motion and Final Hearing: After the cooling-off period expires, both parties appear before the court to confirm that they still wish to proceed with the divorce.

The Cooling-Off Period be waived?
In SSC *Amardeep Singh v. Harveen Kaur* (2017). the six-month cooling-off period under Section 13B(2) of the Hindu Marriage Act is is not mandatory and can be waived by discretion .

False Dowry Cases Against Husbands and Misuse of the Domestic Violence Act: A Legal Perspective

The legislative intent behind Section 498A of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (now Section 85/86 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023) and the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 ("DV Act") was to safeguard married women from cruelty and domestic abuse. However, over the years, Indian courts, including the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India, have repeatedly observed that these provisions are susceptible to misuse as instruments of personal vendetta, harassment, and extortion against husbands and their families.

Child Custody Rights

Indian courts follow the principle of "best interest of the child" when deciding custody matters. However, there is a strong legal presumption that children below the age of five should remain with the mother. Under the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956, while the father is considered the natural guardian, the mother's right to custody—especially of young children—is well-established.

Courts consider factors such as the emotional bond between parent and child, financial stability, the child's preference (if the child is old enough), and the overall environment each parent can provide. Women should know that being a homemaker or having limited income does not disqualify them from custody. The father can be directed to provide financial support for the child's upbringing.

ANTICIPATORY BAIL IN FRAUD AND FORGERY CASE

Present case is Anticipatory Bail Application filed apprehending arrest in FIR for offences u/s. 420, 465, 467, 468, 479 r/w. 34 of IPC. Applicant introduced accused no. 2 land broker to first informant. It is alleged that Applicant was one of the beneficiaries under the aforesaid land transaction. Further, documentation prepared and facilitated turned out to be forged and fabricated since informant was unable to mutate their names in the land revenue records pertains to said land parcel as the land purchased by them was tribal land hence there was embargo. 

Court observed that, there is unexplained delay of 4-5 years in filing FIR. Further most of allegations are against Accused no. 2. Rights of parties were governed by Agreements and other documents. The applicant’s role was limited to introduce parties and facilitating preliminary steps which does not amount to offence u/s. 420 IPC. Prima facie the dispute between parties is of a civil nature coupled with absence of essential ingredients of the alleged Sections. It is not the prosecution case that Applicant participated in forgery. The allegations appeared to be related to a failed investment and land acquisition transactions and subsequent grievance is predominantly of a civil nature. Thus custodial interrogation of applicant neither warranted nor necessary in facts especially when accused no.2 already enlarged on bail. Anticipatory Bail granted to applicant.

Bombay High Cout

UNILATERAL CONVEYANCE OF PLOT

THE CASE:
Competent authority has granted certificate in favour of Housing Society for unilateral conveyance deed. The Developer - Plaintiff has questioned its validity before City Civil Court. The stay was granted in the said suit and hence the present appellant has challenged the same in appeal.

ARGUMENTS:
It was contented by the Developer that, in the agreement for sale executed with flat purchaser it was agreed to create lease interest in respect of portion of larger plot and not whole plot.

The question falls for consideration was “whether competent authority granting unilateral execution of conveyance deed in respect of larger plot was in accordance with agreements executed?

As per section 10 and 11 of MOFA Act Competent Authority is to perform duty and obligation which Promoter is to perform under law i.e. to convey title and execute documents. The entitlement of exact quantification of FSI on the plot cannot be gone into in proceedings. 

CONCLUSION:
Court determined that, agreement format was prescribed for first time in 1986, therefore question of conveyance as per agreement does not arise. It is observed that, constructed area of building is disproportionate to the area of building agreed to convey. Therefore, Court confirmed the Competent Authority’s order of unilateral conveyance of larger plot. 

Bombay High Court

RIGOROUS IMPRISONMENT IN CHEQUE BOUNCING CASE

On request of accused complainant paid Rs.2,50,000/- to accused as a hand-loan on 28.12.2004. Accused issued post-dated cheque. Complainant deposited the cheque in the Bank which was dishonoured on account of insufficient funds. Hence after issue of notice complainant filed a complaint u/s. 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act.	

During trial accused pleaded not guilty however he admitted to have issued cheque. He contended that it was issued on 01.02.2004 and the complainant altered it to 31.12.2004. The cheque dated 01.02.2004, therefore, barred by limitation.

Trial court recorded conviction u/s. 138 of the N.I. Act and sentenced the accused to undergo imprisonment for three months along with compensation.

Appellate court confirmed conviction of trial court but set aside the rigorous imprisonment of 3 months without assigning any reason. Accused was not shown as handicapped nor he was above 55 years of age. Therefore, leniency shown by appellate court was not justified hence judgement set aside.

Bombay High Court

RECOURSE WHEN POLICE REFUSE TO REGISTER FIR

Section 175(3) of Bharatiya Nagrik Suraksha Sanhita - BNSS (section 156(3) of CRPC) is used when police refuse to register the FIR. Protest Petition can be filed by Victim when police submit negative report refusing to register FIR. It is filed by the Victim when Police submit negative report for closure of case. Protest Petition aims to ensure justice by issuing directions to Police to register FIR upon hearing.

The Protest Petition usually filed before Police register FIR. The Magistrate has power under BNSS section to hold investigation or preliminary inquiry when report u/s. 176 of BNSS is received. 

Protest Petition is treated as complaint, it allows the victim to lead the evidence so that Magistrate can take cognizance and order investigation.

This provision is very important as it safeguard the justice to the victim and increase Police accountability for FIR registration and investigation.

This mechanism administer justice where police fail to act or where police ignore Magistrate’s order. Hence it provides recourse for inaction.

KNOW WHETHER TRANSFERRING MINOR’S PROPERTY IS AN OFFENCE


In the case before hand complainant is the owner of the piece of land and he is in possession. He came to know that, father transferred minor’s (his) property to society without obtaining permission from competent court and repurchase it back from society. Therefore, criminal complaint was filed alleging that, accused has committed criminal breach of trust and prepared false documents and executed will deed. 

It is alleged that, property transferred favouring society was without legal necessity. Further society was controlled by accused only and society later on transferred back the said land in favour of accused. Hence there was dishonest intention since inception. It is submitted that, alienation of minor’s property is voidable at his instance. FIR cumulatively shows that all the accused conspired together to cheat minor to cause wrongful gain and wrongful loss to minor. 

Accused advocate submitted that, if we consider all the allegations of FIR, still it does not disclose any material showing forgery or cheating. FIR filed 35 later years after attaining majority by minor and after 48 years of executing documents against 78 years old father and 74 years mother and to apply pressure and harass them. Therefore, FIR held liable to be quashed.

featured_reviews.name: Ganesh Raut
featured_reviews.review_text:
I recently completed a property transaction and was searching for a trustworthy advocate to help me prepare all the necessary legal documents. After researching for nearly 10-15 days, I was fortunate to come across Advocate Mr. Vijay Chavan—a familiar face from my past, as we once played kabaddi together. This unexpected connection immediately put me at ease.

From our first meeting, Mr.Vijay Chavan impressed me with his professionalism, deep knowledge of property law, and genuine care for his clients. He patiently listened to every detail about my property and the deal I was making. What truly stood out was his ability to explain complex legal terms in a simple, understandable way, and his willingness to answer all my questions—no matter how small.

Mr.Vijay Chavan not only guided me on which documents to prepare but also provided valuable suggestions to ensure that my interests were protected, even in case of any future legal challenges. His advice was always practical and in my best interest, and he made sure that every legal aspect was thoroughly covered before I moved forward.

Throughout the process, he was polite, approachable, and always available for support. He handled discussions with the property seller with professionalism and kindness, which made the transaction smooth and stress-free for me. I truly appreciate his dedication, honesty, and the personal attention he gave to my case.

If you are looking for an advocate who combines expertise with empathy, and who will stand by you every step of the way, I highly recommend Mr. Vijay Chavan. His guidance not only gave me confidence but also peace of mind during an important milestone in my life. Thank you, sir, for your exceptional support and for treating my case as if it were your own.

Advisable note :- Always consult a knowledgeable advocate like Mr. Chavan before any property transaction. Their expertise can save you from future hassles and ensure your investment is legally secure.
